channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Using AI in the global fight against HIV
item.description: When faced with the possibility of an HIV diagnosis, sometimes the best initial prescription is support from a trusted friend—someone who might offer not just emotional guidance but also critical, practical health resources. A Harvard research team thinks artificial intelligence has a role to play in that process.

item.title: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods show stronger brain responses to appetizing foods
item.description: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) show stronger responses in the brain's reward network when viewing images of appetizing foods—and these brain responses are linked to increases in body fat one year later.

item.title: AI breast cancer survival model could improve accuracy and personalize care
item.description: New University of Cincinnati Cancer Center research published in the Journal of Statistical Theory and Practice describes the potential for a more robust and accurate breast cancer survival model that combines statistical methods with a deep learning framework. The goal is to give physicians a better tool to make personalized care decisions for each patient.

item.title: Tackling diabetes with an electronic implant: How a tiny catalyst lowers blood sugar
item.description: Type 2 diabetes is becoming increasingly common worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, it is often linked to obesity, a sedentary lifestyle and excess energy intake over many years. Although insulin injections can bring blood sugar levels down, they do not address the body's chronic energy surplus. Insulin merely helps muscle cells take up glucose from the bloodstream, but if the body does not use that energy, the excess is converted into fat. This helps explain why many patients continue to gain weight despite treatment.

item.title: AI tool may support dermatologists in assessing skin lesions for cancer risk
item.description: Mayo Clinic researchers have found that an artificial intelligence (AI) tool may provide dermatologists with additional information to help assess whether skin lesions are cancerous and inform their clinical decisions about whether to biopsy or monitor them, according to a study published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings.

item.title: The tendency to imitate others is shared across 22 countries, study finds
item.description: People often imitate some of the actions and gestures of others they are observing, without deliberately trying to do so. This tendency, known as automatic imitation, has long been assumed to be universal.

item.title: Who decides when medical AI may be updated?
item.description: Medical AI can improve with new patient data, but every update must be checked first. Patients, equipment and ways of working change, and a model trained on older data can gradually get worse without anyone noticing.

item.title: Gut microbiome may help explain why sleep improvement varies after hydrogen supplementation
item.description: A Hiroshima University–led clinical trial found that hydrogen supplementation did not significantly improve sleep quality compared with a placebo; however, exploratory analyses suggest that differences in the abundance of hydrogen-producing gut bacteria may be associated with individual differences in sleep-related responses.

item.title: How much autonomy do women actually have when giving birth?
item.description: You spend your pregnancy researching and planning for when your baby finally arrives, as well as considering what might happen if things don't go according to plan.

item.title: 4 ways to help your body adjust to the fall time change
item.description: An extra hour in bed sounds like a good deal. But while our phones may update to the fall time change automatically, our body clock isn't quite so quick. You may even find yourself waking up earlier than normal and ready for bed before your evening has properly begun.

item.title: Women are more optimistic about aging—until memory problems emerge
item.description: A study, published in the Journal of Women & Aging, found memory complaints were linked to negative expectations about aging in people with mild cognitive impairment as well as cognitively healthy adults.

item.title: Plant-first food pyramid brings international dietary guidelines together in adaptable global guide
item.description: Dietary guidance varies by country, and no international food pyramid has brought its recommendations together until now. BYU nutritional science professor Karen Della Corte led a global team of nutrition scientists to develop an International Food Guide Pyramid that reflects broad scientific agreement and can be adapted across cultures and borders.

item.title: Updated cancer treatment framework offers new guidance on actionability and resistance biomarkers
item.description: ESMO has published version 2 of the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (ESCAT), a major update to the internationally recognized precision oncology framework that helps oncologists assess the clinical relevance of molecular alterations and match patients with the most appropriate targeted therapies.

item.title: Can Reddit help strengthen health communications on extreme heat?
item.description: Two years ago, Robbie M. Parks, an environmental health scientist at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, and Nathaniel Matthews-Trigg, director of climate and disaster resilience at Americares, founded an online community on Reddit, r/heat_prep, where members share information and advice about coping with extreme temperatures.

item.title: Mindfulness and self-compassion can alleviate premenstrual symptoms
item.description: A kind attitude toward oneself and practicing mindfulness can improve functioning in individuals who experience severe premenstrual symptoms, according to a study by psychologists from SWPS University and Jagiellonian University.

item.title: Blood test can help clinicians better identify brain injury severity in patients
item.description: Clinician-scientists hope to expand the use of blood-based biomarker tests for traumatic brain injury (TBI) to improve identification and escalation of care for patients whose diagnosis otherwise might be missed.

item.title: First-of-its-kind trial tests low-dose radiation to target brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease
item.description: Mayo Clinic researchers are studying whether low-dose radiation therapy can slow the progression of Parkinson's disease by targeting inflammation in areas of the brain affected by the disease. The clinical trial is the first to investigate low-dose radiation as an anti-inflammatory approach in patients with early-stage Parkinson's disease.

item.title: Discrimination fuels mental health crisis among LGBTQ+ youth, national report finds
item.description: LGBTQ+ youth continue to face high rates of anxiety, depression and suicidal thoughts, driven by ongoing discrimination, a new report says.

item.title: Researchers show how leukemia cells 'hide' from treatment
item.description: In a first-of-its-kind study collaboration, new research has uncovered that chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) cells may switch between different survival signals, helping explain why treatments work well for some patients but stop working for others. These findings could ultimately help pave the way for more personalized treatment.

item.title: Clinical support tool helps primary care health professionals detect and treat chronic kidney disease
item.description: Investigators have developed and validated a clinical decision support tool to improve the diagnosis and treatment of chronic kidney disease (CKD) at the point of care. The research was presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

item.title: Potassium binder may ease the burden of dietary potassium restriction in people on dialysis
item.description: Dietary potassium restriction is important for managing hyperkalemia, or high blood potassium levels, in individuals on maintenance hemodialysis, but it imposes a substantial day-to-day burden. Results from a recent clinical trial indicate that adding the potassium binder sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) may help. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

item.title: Fruits and vegetables outperform medication for treating metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease
item.description: In people with chronic kidney disease (CKD), oral sodium bicarbonate is a standard treatment for metabolic acidosis (too much acid buildup in the body), but results from a recent clinical trial indicate that dietary acid reduction with base-producing fruits and vegetables may be a better option. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

item.title: Social determinants linked with kidney failure risk among survivors of critical illness and acute kidney injury
item.description: New research indicates that certain individual- and neighborhood-level social determinants of health may increase the risk of developing postdischarge kidney failure in patients who developed acute kidney injury while in intensive care. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026 Oct. 22–25.

item.title: Standardized kidney biopsy protocol is safe in high-risk patients
item.description: Results from a prospective study reveal that with standardized precautions, even high-risk patients may safely undergo a kidney biopsy, a cornerstone of kidney diagnostics that is often perceived as dangerous in certain vulnerable patient populations. The findings were presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

item.title: US cannabis legalization linked to rise in cardiovascular hospital admissions
item.description: Legalization of recreational cannabis in the U.S. is associated with a rise in hospital admissions for cardiovascular disease, finds an analysis of more than 50 million patient discharge records, published in the open-access journal BMJ Open.

item.title: Early uptake for oral semaglutide proves rapid relative to injectables
item.description: Early uptake was rapid for oral semaglutide (Wegovy pill) relative to injectable incretin-based weight management therapies, according to a study published online Oct. 13 in Annals of Internal Medicine.

item.title: Beyond the ACE score: A single number may miss the complexity of childhood trauma, study suggests
item.description: For years, childhood trauma has often been measured with a simple score. The widely used adverse childhood experiences, or ACEs, system assigns points for experiences such as abuse, neglect, parental divorce, substance abuse in the home and other adversities before age 18. In general, the higher the score, the greater the risk for future health and behavioral problems.

item.title: ADHD medication unlikely to raise risk of self-harm, international study finds
item.description: The risk of self-harm among people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is highest before people start ADHD medication, rather than after treatment begins, according to new research led by Aston University and recently published in the journal BMJ Mental Health.

item.title: Adults with type 1 diabetes more likely to have depressive, anxiety symptoms
item.description: Adults with type 1 diabetes have a higher prevalence of depressive and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) symptoms than those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes, according to a research letter published online Oct. 20 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

item.title: Nurses are an important resource in Swedish bowel cancer screening
item.description: Colonoscopies performed by specially trained nurses as part of the Swedish bowel cancer screening program are of at least the same quality as those performed by doctors, according to a study from Karolinska Institutet published in the journal Endoscopy. The results suggest that nurses could help to address the increasing demand for examinations within the national screening program.
